name: TimescaleDB
license: Apache 2.0 (core) and Tiger Data License (full Community Edition)
summary: A PostgreSQL extension that turns ordinary tables into time-partitioned, compressed time-series tables.
intro: TimescaleDB is not a separate database. It is an extension you load into PostgreSQL, so you keep SQL, joins with your other tables, transactions, existing drivers and tools. You mark a table as a hypertable, and behind the scenes it splits rows into chunks by time, seven days each by default. Inserts land in the newest chunk, queries skip chunks outside their time range, and dropping old data means dropping whole chunks instead of deleting rows one by one.

Older chunks can be converted to a columnstore, which groups values by column and compresses them, so scans over long periods read far less data. Continuous aggregates keep rollups such as hourly averages up to date as new rows arrive, and background policies handle compression and retention on a schedule. These features belong to the Community Edition under the Tiger Data License, which is free to self-host but may not be offered as a hosted service. The Apache 2.0 edition has only the basics, such as hypertables. The company behind it renamed itself from Timescale to Tiger Data in June 2025 and runs the hosted Tiger Cloud.
strengths: It’s still PostgreSQL: full SQL, joins with business tables, and the same backups and tools
Automatic time partitioning with cheap chunk-level retention
Columnstore compression and continuous aggregates keep long-range queries fast
New syntax (since 2.20) makes a hypertable with plain `CREATE TABLE ... WITH (tsdb.hypertable)`
limits: Columnstore, continuous aggregates and retention policies need the Tiger Data License edition, so managed Postgres services that ship only the Apache edition lack them
Writes scale up on one PostgreSQL primary rather than out across many nodes
You still operate PostgreSQL underneath: connections, vacuum, upgrades and extension versions

story: Ajay Kulkarni and Mike Freedman first ran iobeam, an Internet of Things data platform. It collected time-series data from more than 100,000 devices, and the off-the-shelf time-series databases they tried didn’t meet their needs. The usual advice was that relational databases couldn’t scale to time-series volumes, which is why NoSQL time-series stores existed, but those stores gave up the secondary indexes, rich queries and joins that made SQL useful.

So they built time-series storage on top of PostgreSQL instead. People took an interest in the database before the company changed course, and in early 2017 the founders relaunched it as Timescale. Kulkarni announced TimescaleDB on April 4, 2017, and two weeks later Freedman took a “somewhat heretical stance”: that relational databases can be quite powerful for time-series data, if you solve the scaling problem. TimescaleDB 1.0 followed in October 2018.

In December 2018 Timescale began splitting features between an Apache 2.0 core and a source-available Timescale License that bars offering them as a hosted database service, aimed at cloud vendors who sell open-source software without funding it. Native compression arrived in 2019. In June 2025 the company renamed itself Tiger Data, keeping the TimescaleDB name for the extension.

choices.choice: An extension inside PostgreSQL, not a new database
choices.why: Users keep full SQL, joins with their business tables, and every existing driver and tool. The founders were frank that “PostgreSQL was the only database that we wanted to use.”

choices.choice: Chunks by time, sized to fit in memory
choices.why: A plain table slows down once its indexes outgrow RAM, because each insert may read and write 8 KB pages on disk. Time-series inserts land mostly in the latest interval, so splitting by time keeps the active chunk and its indexes in memory.

choices.choice: Keep B-tree indexes instead of LSM trees
choices.why: NoSQL time-series stores used log-structured merge trees for fast writes, at the cost of more memory and weak secondary indexes. Chunking let TimescaleDB keep PostgreSQL’s ordinary indexes and still sustain high insert rates.
Old chunks are rarely updated, so 1.5 began rolling their rows into per-column arrays compressed with type-specific methods, such as delta-of-delta for timestamps and Gorilla compression for floats.
